old: It once named the gates thought to hold back the waters of the sky.
A portcullis-like blockage lent its name to a clouding of the eye's lens.
Greek katar(rh)áktēs, meaning both 'waterfall' and 'portcullis,' underlies both of this word's modern meanings.
clues: This medical term first meant the floodgates of heaven, coming from an ancient Greek word for water rushing downwards.
It is a clouding of the eye's lens that blurs vision, common with age and fixed by lens-replacement surgery, unlike glaucoma, which involves pressure on the optic nerve.
The same word names a mighty, thundering waterfall, and medicine borrowed it for the eye because a clouded lens was likened to a portcullis shutting out light.
